verdict.rationale: Three independent witnesses across poetry, prophecy, and narrative converge on one lexical pattern. Psalm 139:7-10 builds a double merism (a two-part figure naming the extremes to mean the whole), pairing heaven (shamayim, H8064) with the grave (sheol, H7585), and the wings of dawn (shachar, H7837) with the farthest sea (yam, H3220), exhausting the spatial extremes, and at each pole the locative 'there' (sham, H8033) asserts the same finding, you are there. Jeremiah 23:24 puts the claim in a first-person divine oracle with the verb 'fill' (male, H4390) governing both 'heaven' (shamayim, H8064) and 'earth' (erets, H0776) under one direct-object marker (eth, H0853), so that no person can 'hide' (sathar, H5641). Acts 17:27-28 carries the field into Greek with 'far' (makran, G3112), the participle 'existing' (huparcho, G5225), and the triad 'in' (en, G1722) him we 'live' (zao, G2198), 'move' (kineo, G2795), and 'are' (eimi, G1510), while 'Maker' (poietes, G4163) holds Creator and creation apart. The one boundary the words leave is that the same canon also speaks of a special covenantal presence, dwelling, drawing near, hiding the face, which the vocabulary holds together with the omnipresence of essence without ranking the two. No variant unit unsettles the verdict and the merism vocabulary recurs intact in Amos 9:2-3, so the pattern is pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible) and decisive on the proposition's main claim.

scripture.force: Two parallel rhetorical questions, each opened by 'where' (an, H0575), ask where the speaker could go from God's 'Spirit' (ruach, H7307) and flee from his 'presence' or 'face' (panim, H6440). The queried tokens confirm the doubled 'where' (an) plus the verb 'flee' (barach, H1272). The grammar presupposes the answer no such destination exists, so the question itself encodes the omnipresence claim.

A vertical merism (a two-part figure naming the extremes to mean the whole) pairs 'heaven' (shamayim, H8064), the highest place, with 'the grave' or 'underworld' (sheol, H7585), the lowest. The locative 'there' (sham, H8033) plus the particle 'behold you' (hinnekka) asserts divine presence at each pole. The speaker's verbs are conditional (an 'if-then' clause structure), if I ascend, if I make my bed, but the presence asserted by 'there' (sham) is unconditional.

A horizontal merism (a two-part figure naming the extremes to mean the whole) pairs the 'wings' (kanaph, H3671) of the 'dawn' (shachar, H7837) in the east with the farthest 'sea' (yam, H3220) in the west. The image presses the geographic limit case to test the claim of the previous verse.

Even at the prior verse's farthest point, the locative 'there' (sham, H8033) resumes and the divine 'hand' (yad, H3027) leads while the right hand 'grasps' or 'holds' (achaz, H0270) the speaker. The repetition of 'there' (sham) from verse 8 closes the frame of presence across every extreme just named.

A first-person divine oracle, marked 'declaration of YHWH' (neum YHWH), poses a rhetorical question contrasting 'near' (qarob, H7138) with 'far' (rachoq, H7350). The ETCBC clause analysis (a Hebrew Bible syntax database) tags the unit a question with predicate-complement constituents, the structure of a self-disclosure that denies God can be a merely local, nearby deity unaware of the distant.

The queried tokens confirm the verb 'fill' (male, H4390) with first-person divine subject taking both 'heaven' (shamayim, H8064) and 'earth' (erets, H0776) under the direct-object marker (eth, H0853), denying that any person can 'hide' (sathar, H5641) in secret places. The interrogative particle (a question marker) on the verb makes the assertion emphatic, a denial framed as a question.

Paul states a purpose, that they might 'seek' (zeteo, G2212) God and perhaps 'grope after' (pselaphao, G5584) and 'find' (heurisko, G2147) him. The clause then adds, and indeed he is not 'far' (makran, G3112) from each one of us, with the participle 'existing' (huparcho, G5225). The queried Greek confirms 'far' (makran) plus 'existing' (huparcho) asserting nearness to every individual.

The triad 'in' (en, G1722) him we 'live' (zao, G2198), and 'move' (kineo, G2795), and 'are' (eimi, G1510), locates creaturely life, motion, and being inside God. The queried tokens confirm 'in' (en), 'live' (zao), 'move' (kineo), and 'are' (eimi) in the verse. The Creator-creature distinction is held by 'Maker' (poietes, G4163) language in the same speech, where God is the one who made the world, so the 'in' (en) is location not identity.

A prophetic oracle reuses the same merism (a two-part figure naming the extremes to mean the whole) vocabulary. The queried tokens show 'the grave' (sheol, H7585) and 'heaven' (shamayim, H8064) as the dig-down and climb-up extremes, with the locative 'there' (sham, H8033) asserting that even there the divine hand reaches. This is the Psalm 139 pattern recurring in a different genre, which corroborates the verdict pan-canonically (spread across the whole Bible).

Cain goes out from the 'presence' or 'face' (panim, H6440) of YHWH and dwells in the land of Nod. The queried tokens confirm 'presence' (panim) here. The same word that Psalm 139:7 uses for the presence one cannot flee is used for a relational, cultic departure, which shows the vocabulary carries two senses, spatial omnipresence and covenantal nearness, that the canon does not collapse into each other.

complicating_texts.resolution: Solomon asks whether God can dwell on earth when the heavens and the highest heaven cannot 'contain' (kul, H3557) him. The queried tokens confirm 'contain' (kul) governing 'heaven' (shamayim, H8064) alongside 'earth' (erets, H0776) and the house being built. The container language denies any spatial bounding of God while affirming a real, non-exclusive temple presence, so it reinforces rather than contradicts the verdict.

Cain departs from the 'presence' or 'face' (panim, H6440) of YHWH. The queried tokens confirm 'presence' (panim) here. The idiom names covenantal favor and cultic locale, not ontological absence (absence of being). The same 'presence' (panim) that one cannot flee in Psalm 139:7 is the 'presence' (panim) one can leave relationally here, so the word carries a special-presence sense alongside the omnipresence-of-essence sense without ranking them.

Jonah flees from the 'presence' or 'face' (panim, H6440) of YHWH toward Tarshish, and the queried tokens confirm 'presence' (panim) twice plus a flight verb, the very pair from Psalm 139:7. The narrative then has YHWH hurl a wind on the sea in the next verse, so the attempted flight is shown futile by the storyline itself, confirming omnipresence by counter-example.

The oracle says that even if they 'hide' (sathar, H5641) on the top of Carmel or at the bottom of the 'sea' (yam, H3220), God will search and seize them. The queried tokens confirm 'hide' (sathar) and 'sea' (yam) here. The verse is a complicating-looking flight scenario that the text itself resolves against the fugitive, so it supports the verdict rather than unsettling it.

variants.note: Acts 17:27-28 sits outside the ingested ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) window (3 John 1:1 to 1:15), so no CBGM apparatus (the genealogical method for tracing manuscript readings) was examined. Known minor witnesses vary on the article with 'God' (theos) and on the optative form (a Greek mood expressing wish or possibility), but none touches the 'far' (makran), 'in' (en), or 'existing' (huparcho) vocabulary that carries the verdict. Psalm 139 and Jeremiah 23 are Old Testament and outside ECM scope. The verdict holds across all plausible readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads 'fill' (male, H4390) and the merism (the extremes-naming figure) plus the 'in him we live' (en, G1722) language as predicating unbounded spatial presence of the divine being itself. On this reading God is wholly present at every point, and the near and far oracle of Jeremiah 23:23-24 forecloses any local-deity limitation. The vocabulary directly supports this as the proposition's main claim.

Stresses that the same canon uses a distinct register for a localized, manifest presence, dwelling in the temple in 1 Kings 8, drawing near, going out from the 'presence' or 'face' (panim, H6440) in Genesis 4:16 and Jonah 1:3, hiding the face. On this reading the words affirm omnipresence of essence but leave the manner of God's special presence as a further category the lexicon marks but does not rank against the first. This lens is represented in its strongest form, it does not deny omnipresence, it adds that presence is spoken of in more than one mode.

Reads Acts 17:28, 'in' (en, G1722) him we live and move and are, as locating creation within God, which the preposition 'in' (en) allows. But the same speech keeps 'Maker' (poietes, G4163) and the world-making language, so the lexical context blocks an ontological identification (an identification at the level of being) of God with creation. The reading is fairly stated, it captures a real feature of the 'in' (en) clause, but the surrounding vocabulary limits how far it can be pressed.

Would erase the Creator-creature line that Jeremiah 23, God 'fills' (male, H4390) versus persons 'hide' (sathar, H5641), and Acts 17, 'Maker' (poietes, G4163) versus made, both keep. The lexical pattern preserves the distinction the proposition requires, so a strict identification of God with the world is not supported by the words.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict rests on grammatico-historical reading (interpreting the text by its grammar and original historical setting) of three independent texts plus the corroborating Amos 9 echo. The two-part proposition, present everywhere yet distinct from creation, is held by reading the spatial 'fill' (male, H4390) and merism (the extremes-naming figure) language together with the explicit 'Maker' (poietes, G4163) vocabulary in each context. The honest residue is that the canon also speaks of a special covenantal presence, which the lenses above register without the words ranking essence-presence above manifest-presence.

stem_audit.notes: The proposition restates the lexical pattern, fully present everywhere, not bounded by space, while remaining distinct from creation, without importing a tradition-specific taxonomy (a labeling system tied to one school of thought). The 'fill' (male, H4390) and merism (the extremes-naming figure) vocabulary and the 'Maker' (poietes, G4163) language match both halves of the statement, so the verdict is derived from the text and not smuggled by the stem.

lay_summary: Three passages spread across the Bible make the same claim with different words. Psalm 139 verses 7 to 10 lists every spatial extreme a person could reach, up to the heavens (shamayim), down to the grave (sheol), east to the wings of dawn (shachar), west to the farthest sea (yam), and at each pole the answer is the same little word 'there' (sham), you are there, your hand leads me. The verb 'to flee' (barach) is used precisely because the questions assume no destination outside God exists. Jeremiah 23 verse 24 puts the claim in God's own voice with the verb 'to fill' (male), which takes both heaven and earth together under one object marker, the grammatical signature of unbounded presence, and adds that no one can 'hide' (sathar) in secret places. Acts 17 verses 27 and 28 carry the same idea into Greek, God is not 'far' (makran) from each one of us, and 'in' (en) him we 'live' (zao) and 'move' (kineo) and 'exist' (eimi), while the word 'Maker' (poietes) in the same speech keeps the Creator and the creation apart, so being in him means located, not identical. The same heaven, grave, sea, and hide vocabulary returns in Amos 9, which is why the pattern is decisive rather than isolated. So the words clearly affirm both halves, present everywhere, yet distinct from what he fills and made. Where readers can still diverge is not over whether God is everywhere but over how to relate this to a second kind of language the same canon uses, a special covenantal presence that can be drawn near, dwelt in at the temple, departed from, as when Cain goes out from the 'presence' (panim) of the LORD and Jonah flees from the 'presence' (panim) of the LORD. The vocabulary marks both a presence of being that is everywhere and a presence of relationship that can be near or withdrawn, and it holds them together without ever ranking one above the other. That single unranked pairing is the only room the text leaves, and it does not touch the central affirmation.
